subject: history
title: The Russian Revolutions of 1917: from a women's bread strike to Bolshevik power
dek: In 1917 Russia went through two revolutions in eight months. The first began on International Women's Day, when women textile workers in Petrograd walked out of their factories to protest bread shortages, and within a week the three-hundred-year-old Romanov dynasty was gone. The second, in October, put Lenin's Bolshevik party in power and led to a civil war, a one-party state and the Soviet Union. This lesson explains how a failing empire at war collapsed, why the liberal Provisional Government could not hold on, how the Bolsheviks took power, what the revolution promised and delivered for women, and how 1917 looked from Beijing, Tokyo and Taipei.
honesty: Russia still used the Julian calendar in 1917, which ran thirteen days behind the Gregorian calendar used in Western Europe. This lesson gives Russian (Old Style) dates for events inside Russia, as historians usually do, and adds the Western date where it matters. That is why the 'February' Revolution began on 8 March and the 'October' Revolution took place on 7 November by the Western calendar. Figures for crowd sizes, election results and civil war deaths vary between sources; this lesson gives rounded figures and ranges rather than precise numbers. The meaning of 1917, whether a popular revolution, a coup by a small party, or both, is still argued over, and the lesson presents the main positions without settling the debate.

timeline.label: Bloody Sunday
timeline.detail: Troops fire on a peaceful march led by the priest Georgy Gapon in St Petersburg, starting the 1905 Revolution.

timeline.label: October Manifesto
timeline.detail: Nicholas II promises civil liberties and an elected parliament, the Duma, to end a general strike.

timeline.label: Russia enters the First World War
timeline.detail: St Petersburg is renamed Petrograd to sound less German. Huge losses follow in 1914 and 1915.

timeline.label: The tsar takes command
timeline.detail: Nicholas II becomes commander-in-chief and leaves for the front, leaving the Empress Alexandra and her favourite Rasputin with influence in the capital.

timeline.label: Rasputin murdered
timeline.detail: Aristocrats led by Prince Felix Yusupov kill Grigory Rasputin in Petrograd.

timeline.label: International Women's Day strike
timeline.detail: Women textile workers in Petrograd strike over bread (8 March by the Western calendar). Within days the strike becomes general.

timeline.label: The garrison mutinies
timeline.detail: Soldiers refuse to fire on crowds and join them. The Petrograd Soviet and a Duma committee form on the same day.

timeline.label: Nicholas II abdicates
timeline.detail: A Provisional Government under Prince Georgy Lvov takes office. 'Dual power' with the Soviet begins.

timeline.label: Women's suffrage march
timeline.detail: Tens of thousands of women march in Petrograd to demand the vote. The Provisional Government grants women the vote in the summer.

timeline.label: Lenin returns
timeline.detail: Lenin arrives at the Finland Station after crossing Germany by train and presents his April Theses.

timeline.label: July Days
timeline.detail: Armed demonstrations in Petrograd fail. Lenin goes into hiding and Kerensky becomes prime minister.

timeline.label: Kornilov affair
timeline.detail: General Lavr Kornilov's move against Petrograd collapses, discrediting Kerensky and strengthening the Bolsheviks.

timeline.label: October Revolution
timeline.detail: The Military Revolutionary Committee takes Petrograd and the Winter Palace (6–8 November, Western calendar). The Second Congress of Soviets passes decrees on peace and land.

timeline.label: Constituent Assembly elections
timeline.detail: The Socialist Revolutionaries win the most votes; the Bolsheviks win about a quarter.

timeline.label: The Cheka is founded
timeline.detail: Felix Dzerzhinsky heads the new political police.

timeline.label: Constituent Assembly dispersed
timeline.detail: The elected assembly meets once and is closed by the Bolsheviks.

timeline.label: Calendar change
timeline.detail: Soviet Russia adopts the Gregorian calendar; 31 January is followed by 14 February.

timeline.label: Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
timeline.detail: Soviet Russia leaves the war, giving up large western territories to Germany and its allies.

timeline.label: The Romanovs are killed
timeline.detail: Nicholas, Alexandra, their five children and four servants are shot in Yekaterinburg.

timeline.label: Civil War
timeline.detail: Reds fight Whites, nationalist movements, peasant armies and foreign interventions. Several million people die, most from hunger and disease.

timeline.label: Abortion legalised
timeline.detail: Soviet Russia becomes the first country to legalise abortion on request.

timeline.label: Kronstadt and NEP
timeline.detail: Sailors at Kronstadt revolt and are crushed. Lenin introduces the New Economic Policy, allowing some private trade.

timeline.label: USSR founded
timeline.detail: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics is formally created.

timeline.label: Lenin dies
timeline.detail: A struggle for succession begins, which Stalin wins by the end of the decade.

sections.title: An autocracy that would not share power

blocks.text: At the start of the twentieth century the Russian Empire was the largest country in the world, stretching from Poland to the Pacific. It was ruled by Tsar Nicholas II of the Romanov dynasty, which had held the throne since 1613. Nicholas believed that God had given him unlimited power and that his duty was to pass it on undiminished to his son. There was no national parliament, political parties were illegal, and newspapers were censored.

Underneath this old political system the country was changing quickly. Most Russians were still peasants, and serfdom had been abolished only in 1861. But from the 1890s the state pushed rapid industrialisation, financed by foreign loans and built around railways, mines and huge factories. St Petersburg and Moscow filled with workers who lived in crowded barracks, worked eleven-hour days and had no legal unions. Educated Russians, the intelligentsia, argued about how to change the country, and many turned to revolutionary ideas.

Several revolutionary parties formed. The Socialist Revolutionaries, or SRs, saw the peasants as the core of the revolution and wanted the land given to those who worked it. The Russian Social Democratic Labour Party followed Marx and focused on industrial workers. At its congress in 1903 it split into two factions: the Bolsheviks ('majority'), led by Vladimir Lenin, who wanted a small, disciplined party of professional revolutionaries, and the Mensheviks ('minority'), led by Julius Martov, who favoured a broader, more open party. Liberals, organised from 1905 as the Constitutional Democrats or Kadets, wanted a constitutional monarchy or a parliamentary republic.

The first great warning came in 1905. Russia was losing a war against Japan in Manchuria. On 9 January 1905 a priest named Georgy Gapon led a peaceful march of workers and their families to the Winter Palace to present a petition to the tsar. Troops opened fire and killed many marchers. The day became known as Bloody Sunday, and it set off a year of strikes, mutinies and peasant uprisings. Workers in St Petersburg created a council of elected delegates, a soviet, in which the young Leon Trotsky became a leading figure. To end a general strike, Nicholas issued the October Manifesto, which promised civil liberties and an elected parliament called the Duma.

Nicholas never accepted the Duma as a real partner. He dissolved the first two Dumas quickly and changed the electoral law in 1907 to favour landowners. His prime minister Pyotr Stolypin combined harsh repression with a land reform meant to create a class of independent peasant farmers, but Stolypin was assassinated in 1911. When Russia entered the First World War in August 1914, the regime had survived 1905 without solving any of the problems that caused it.

The war turned these problems into a crisis. The Russian army suffered enormous losses in 1914 and 1915. In September 1915 Nicholas took personal command of the army and moved to headquarters, which meant every defeat was now blamed on him. In Petrograd, as the capital had been renamed, the Empress Alexandra, who was German-born and deeply unpopular, gained influence over appointments. She trusted Grigory Rasputin, a Siberian holy man who seemed able to ease the bleeding of her son Alexei, who had haemophilia. Rumours about Rasputin did great damage to the monarchy's reputation, and in December 1916 a group of aristocrats murdered him. By the winter of 1916–17 trains could not bring enough food and fuel to the cities, prices had risen sharply, and women spent hours in bread queues in the cold.

sections.title: Five days that ended the monarchy

blocks.text: The revolution began on 23 February 1917, which was 8 March by the Western calendar and International Women's Day, a socialist holiday celebrated since 1911. In the Vyborg district of Petrograd, women textile workers walked out of their factories and called on men in the nearby metal works to join them. Local Bolshevik organisers had advised against striking that day because they thought the moment was not right, but the women ignored them. Around ninety thousand workers were on strike by the end of the day, and crowds shouted for bread.

Over the next two days the strike spread across the city until it became a general strike. Students and middle-class residents joined the crowds, and the slogans changed from 'Bread' to 'Down with the war' and 'Down with the autocracy'. Nicholas, at army headquarters in Mogilev, ordered the commander in Petrograd to end the disorders by force. On 26 February soldiers fired on crowds and killed dozens of people.

The turning point came on 27 February. The soldiers of the Petrograd garrison were mostly young peasant recruits and older reservists, and many of them had relatives in the crowds. Starting with the Volhynian Regiment, unit after unit refused to fire, killed or chased away their officers, and joined the demonstrators. Once the army went over to the people, the government had nothing left. Ministers fled or were arrested.

Two new authorities formed on the same day, in two wings of the same building, the Tauride Palace. Members of the Duma created a committee that became the Provisional Government. Socialist activists, mostly Mensheviks and SRs, revived the 1905 model and created the Petrograd Soviet of Workers' and Soldiers' Deputies. On 1 March the Soviet issued its Order No. 1, which told soldiers to elect committees and obey only those orders that did not contradict the Soviet. It badly weakened officers' authority across the army.

Generals and Duma leaders persuaded Nicholas that only his abdication could keep the army fighting. On 2 March 1917 he abdicated for himself and his son. His brother Grand Duke Michael declined the throne the next day. After more than three hundred years, the Romanov monarchy had ended in less than a week, with surprisingly little bloodshed outside Petrograd.

The Provisional Government was led first by Prince Georgy Lvov, a liberal known for his work in local government, with the Kadet historian Pavel Milyukov as foreign minister and the SR lawyer Alexander Kerensky as minister of justice. It quickly introduced freedoms Russia had never had: freedom of speech, press and assembly, an amnesty for political prisoners, the end of religious and ethnic discrimination in law, and the abolition of the death penalty. It promised that a Constituent Assembly elected by universal suffrage would decide the country's permanent constitution.

Real power, however, was shared with the Soviet, which controlled the railways, the telegraph and the loyalty of the soldiers. Lenin later called this situation 'dual power'. Soviets of workers, soldiers and peasants sprang up across the country, along with factory committees and village assemblies. Many people expected the revolution to bring immediate change in their own lives: land for peasants, an eight-hour day and control over factories for workers, peace for soldiers, and self-government for Finns, Ukrainians and other nationalities.

The Provisional Government delayed on almost all of these. It said that land reform and the national question must wait for the Constituent Assembly, and it kept postponing the elections. Most importantly, it kept Russia in the war. In April a note by Milyukov assuring the Allies that Russia would fight to victory caused street protests and forced him to resign. Socialists from the Soviet then joined a coalition government. In June Kerensky, now minister of war, launched a major offensive that collapsed within weeks, and desertion grew rapidly.

Lenin had returned to Petrograd on 3 April after the German government allowed him and other exiles to cross Germany in a sealed train, hoping they would weaken Russia's war effort. At the Finland Station and in his April Theses he called for no support for the Provisional Government, an end to the war, and 'all power to the soviets'. At first even many Bolsheviks thought this was too radical, but his simple slogans of 'peace, land and bread' fitted the mood of the cities and the army better than any other party's programme.

In early July soldiers and workers held armed demonstrations in Petrograd demanding that the Soviet take power. The July Days failed. The government published claims that Lenin was a German agent, arrested several Bolshevik leaders including Trotsky, and Lenin fled to Finland. Kerensky became prime minister. The Bolsheviks seemed beaten.

They were rescued by the Kornilov affair. In late August the army's commander-in-chief, General Lavr Kornilov, sent troops towards Petrograd. Whether he meant to overthrow Kerensky or believed he was acting with Kerensky's approval is still debated. Kerensky turned to the Soviet for help, armed workers' militias, the Red Guards, and released Bolshevik prisoners. Railway workers stopped the troop trains and Kornilov's advance dissolved. Afterwards the right blamed Kerensky for betraying Kornilov and the left suspected him of plotting with him. The Bolsheviks, who had been at the front of the defence, won majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow soviets in September, and Trotsky became chairman of the Petrograd Soviet.

From Finland, Lenin wrote letters insisting that the Bolsheviks must seize power at once, before the Constituent Assembly elections and before Kerensky could recover. On 10 October the Bolshevik Central Committee voted for an armed uprising. Two senior members, Lev Kamenev and Grigory Zinoviev, opposed it and even made their objections public in a newspaper, so the plan was hardly a secret.

The uprising was organised through the Petrograd Soviet's Military Revolutionary Committee, chaired formally by an SR but run largely by Trotsky. Using the defence of the capital as its justification, the committee won the loyalty of most of the garrison. On the night of 24–25 October its forces took bridges, railway stations, the telephone exchange and the state bank with very little fighting. On the morning of 25 October Lenin issued a proclamation that the Provisional Government had been overthrown, although its ministers were still sitting in the Winter Palace. Kerensky had already left the city to look for loyal troops.

The Winter Palace fell in the early hours of 26 October. The cruiser Aurora fired a blank shot as a signal, and some shells were fired from the Peter and Paul Fortress. The palace was defended by military cadets, Cossacks and part of a women's battalion, most of whom drifted away during the evening. The attackers entered and arrested the ministers. Only a few people were killed. The great storming of the Winter Palace that most people picture comes largely from Sergei Eisenstein's film October, made for the tenth anniversary in 1927, and from mass re-enactments staged in 1920.

At the same time the Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets was meeting at the Smolny Institute. Most Mensheviks and right SRs walked out in protest against the seizure of power, which left the Bolsheviks and the Left SRs in control. The congress approved a new government, the Council of People's Commissars, with Lenin as chairman, Trotsky in charge of foreign affairs and Joseph Stalin in charge of nationalities. It passed a Decree on Peace calling for an end to the war without annexations and a Decree on Land that turned landlords' estates over to peasant committees, essentially recognising seizures that peasants were already carrying out.

Moscow fell only after about a week of fighting. Elections to the Constituent Assembly went ahead in November, and they showed the limits of Bolshevik support. The SRs, strongest among the peasants, won the most votes, close to forty percent, while the Bolsheviks won about a quarter, mostly in the cities and the army. When the Assembly met on 5 January 1918 and refused to accept Soviet power, Red Guards closed it the next day and it never met again. Liberal newspapers had already been closed, and in December 1917 a new political police, the Cheka, had been created under Felix Dzerzhinsky.

people.name: Nicholas II
people.text: The last tsar of Russia, who ruled from 1894. He was devoted to his family and to the principle of autocracy, and refused real power-sharing until it was too late. He abdicated in March 1917 and was shot with his family in Yekaterinburg in July 1918.

people.name: Alexandra Feodorovna
people.text: The German-born empress, a granddaughter of Queen Victoria. Her trust in Rasputin and her influence on wartime appointments made her deeply unpopular. She was killed with her family in 1918.

people.name: Grigory Rasputin
people.text: A Siberian peasant mystic who gained the trust of the imperial family because he seemed to help their haemophiliac son. Stories about his influence and private life damaged the monarchy. He was murdered by aristocrats in December 1916.

people.name: Vladimir Lenin
people.text: Leader of the Bolsheviks and the main architect of the October Revolution. He spent most of the years before 1917 in exile in Western Europe. As head of the Soviet government he took Russia out of the war, led it through the civil war and introduced the New Economic Policy. He died after a series of strokes in January 1924.

people.name: Leon Trotsky
people.text: A brilliant speaker and writer who led the St Petersburg Soviet in 1905, joined the Bolsheviks in 1917 and organised the October seizure of power. He then built the Red Army. He lost the power struggle to Stalin, was exiled in 1929 and was murdered in Mexico in 1940 by a Soviet agent.

people.name: Alexander Kerensky
people.text: A lawyer and SR politician who was the only socialist in the first Provisional Government and became its prime minister in July 1917. He fled after October and spent the rest of his long life in exile, mostly in the United States.

people.name: Georgy Lvov
people.text: A liberal prince known for organising local government and wartime relief, and the first head of the Provisional Government from March to July 1917.

people.name: Pavel Milyukov
people.text: A historian and leader of the liberal Kadet party. As foreign minister he wanted to keep fighting for Russia's war aims, and protests over his note to the Allies forced him out in May 1917.

people.name: Julius Martov
people.text: The leader of the Mensheviks and Lenin's former close friend. He opposed the October seizure of power and later criticised Bolshevik repression from exile.

people.name: Viktor Chernov
people.text: The main thinker of the Socialist Revolutionary party and minister of agriculture in 1917. He was elected chairman of the Constituent Assembly on the only day it met.

people.name: Lavr Kornilov
people.text: The army commander-in-chief whose move on Petrograd in August 1917 failed. He later helped found the White Volunteer Army and was killed in 1918.

people.name: Alexandra Kollontai
people.text: A Bolshevik writer and organiser and the leading Marxist theorist of women's liberation in Russia. As People's Commissar of Social Welfare after October 1917 she was one of the first women to serve in a national government. She later headed the Zhenotdel and spent many years as a Soviet diplomat in Norway and Sweden.

people.name: Inessa Armand
people.text: A French-born Bolshevik, close collaborator of Lenin, and the first head of the Zhenotdel, the party's women's department. She died of cholera in 1920.

people.name: Nadezhda Krupskaya
people.text: Lenin's wife and political partner, a specialist in education who worked on literacy and schooling in the Soviet government.

people.name: Maria Bochkareva
people.text: A peasant woman who served in the tsar's army and in 1917 formed the Women's Battalion of Death to shame male soldiers into fighting. She opposed the Bolsheviks, travelled to the United States and Britain to seek support for the Whites, and was executed by the Cheka in 1920.

people.name: Felix Dzerzhinsky
people.text: A Polish-born revolutionary who founded and led the Cheka, the Soviet political police.

people.name: Joseph Stalin
people.text: A Georgian Bolshevik who was People's Commissar for Nationalities after October. In 1922 he became the party's general secretary, the base from which he took power after Lenin's death.

people.name: Georgy Gapon
people.text: The Orthodox priest who led the march of Bloody Sunday in January 1905. He was later killed by revolutionaries who believed he was a police informer.

people.name: John Reed
people.text: An American journalist who witnessed the October Revolution and wrote Ten Days That Shook the World, published in 1919. He died of typhus in Moscow and is buried by the Kremlin wall.

people.name: Sergei Eisenstein
people.text: The Soviet film director whose October (1927) created the most famous images of the storming of the Winter Palace. His work is covered in the lesson on Soviet montage.

sections.title: The vote, the family code and the Zhenotdel

blocks.text: Women started the February Revolution, and the question of what the revolution would do for women ran through all of 1917. Russia had an organised women's rights movement before the war. Its liberal wing, including the League for Women's Equal Rights, had campaigned for the vote since 1905. When the Provisional Government's first plans for the Constituent Assembly elections did not clearly include women, the League organised a large march to the Tauride Palace on 19 March 1917. The marchers, numbering in the tens of thousands, refused to leave until leaders of both the government and the Soviet promised support. During the summer the Provisional Government confirmed the right of women over twenty to vote and stand for office, and Russia became the first great power to give women equal voting rights.

Socialist women had a different emphasis. Kollontai argued that legal equality meant little for a working woman who still did all the housework and childcare and earned less than a man. In her view, women would only be free when society took over cooking, laundry and childcare through public canteens, laundries and nurseries, and when marriage was based on free choice rather than economic dependence. Some of these arguments return decades later in the debates covered in the lesson on Wages for Housework.

The new Soviet government moved quickly on law. Decrees in December 1917 and a family code in 1918 replaced church marriage with civil registration, made divorce easy to obtain for either partner, abolished the legal category of illegitimate children, and declared men and women equal before the law. In November 1920 Soviet Russia became the first country in the world to legalise abortion on request, performed by doctors in hospitals. In 1919 the party created the Zhenotdel, a women's department headed first by Inessa Armand and then by Kollontai, which sent organisers into factories and villages, ran literacy classes and recruited women into local soviets. In Central Asia its activists campaigned against veiling, sometimes at great risk.

The results were uneven. The civil war and famine destroyed the money needed for canteens and nurseries, and easy divorce often left women raising children alone with little support. Many male party members saw women's issues as a distraction. Stalin closed the Zhenotdel in 1930, and in 1936 abortion was banned again, except for medical reasons, as the regime turned to promoting large families. The early Soviet experiment nevertheless influenced feminist and socialist thinking worldwide, and the Soviet state made 8 March an official holiday, which helped fix International Women's Day on that date.

Alexandra Kollontai was born in 1872 into a wealthy noble family in St Petersburg. As a young woman she married an engineer and had a son, but a visit to a huge textile factory near Narva, where she saw how the workers lived, changed her direction. She left her marriage, studied economics in Zurich, and became a Marxist writer. During 1905 she began organising working women and argued with liberal feminists, whom she thought ignored class.

She spent the years from 1908 to 1917 in exile, travelling and speaking across Europe and the United States. She helped promote the idea of an International Women's Day at the socialist women's conference in Copenhagen in 1910, which Clara Zetkin proposed. When the February Revolution broke out on that very day, she was in Norway. She returned to Petrograd in March 1917, joined Lenin in supporting the April Theses, and was arrested after the July Days.

After October she became People's Commissar of Social Welfare. Her ministry was responsible for pensions, the disabled, orphans and maternity care, and she worked on plans for state support for mothers before and after childbirth. Her clash with the Orthodox Church over the Alexander Nevsky Monastery, which she tried to take over for a home for disabled veterans, caused a public outcry. She resigned in March 1918 in protest against the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk.

In the early 1920s she wrote essays and stories about love and sexuality, such as 'Make Way for Winged Eros' and the collection Love of Worker Bees, which made her famous and also made her an easy target for critics who accused her of preaching free love. She supported the Workers' Opposition inside the party in 1921, which argued for more power for trade unions. That cost her influence. From 1923 she was sent abroad as a diplomat, to Norway, Mexico and Sweden, where she served as Soviet envoy and helped negotiate the end of the war between the Soviet Union and Finland in 1944. Diplomacy kept her far from Moscow during Stalin's purges, which killed many of her old comrades. She died in Moscow in 1952.

The Russian Revolution happened in the middle of a world war, and its effects spread quickly. Looking at what else was happening that year shows how many parts of the world were being reshaped at the same time.

items: China: The Republic created by the Xinhai Revolution was falling apart. In July 1917 the general Zhang Xun briefly restored the last emperor, Puyi, for about twelve days. In August the Beijing government declared war on Germany, and Sun Yat-sen set up a rival government in Guangzhou. News of the Bolshevik revolution reached Chinese intellectuals such as Li Dazhao, who wrote about it in 1918. Together with anger at the Paris peace settlement, it fed the May Fourth Movement of 1919, and Soviet advisers helped found the Chinese Communist Party in 1921.

Japan: Japan joined the Allied intervention in Siberia in 1918 and kept troops there until 1922, longer than any other power. In the summer of 1918 the Rice Riots spread across Japan as prices soared, bringing down the government and leading to the first party cabinet under Hara Takashi.

Taiwan: Taiwan was a Japanese colony. After the armed Tapani (Xilai'an) uprising of 1915 was crushed, Taiwanese resistance turned to political and cultural organising. The Taiwanese Cultural Association, founded in 1921, and later leftist groups were influenced by the ideas of national self-determination and socialism that spread after 1917.

United States and Europe: The United States entered the war in April 1917. Britain issued the Balfour Declaration in November 1917, supporting a 'national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine. In 1918 British women over thirty won the vote, and German women won it after the German revolution of November 1918, which was partly inspired by events in Russia.

Mexico: Mexico adopted a new constitution in February 1917, during its own revolution. It included land reform, workers' rights and limits on the church, and it was in some ways more radical on social rights than anything in Europe at the time.

blocks.text: Compared with the Paris Commune of 1871, covered in an earlier lesson, the Bolsheviks drew a clear conclusion: the Commune had failed, Lenin believed, because it had been too hesitant and too democratic in dealing with its enemies. Compared with the Xinhai Revolution of 1911, Russia's revolution went much further, destroying not only the monarchy but the old landowning class and private industry. Chinese revolutionaries of both the Nationalist and Communist parties would study the Bolshevik model of the disciplined party closely.

sections.title: Civil war and the one-party state

blocks.text: The Bolsheviks had promised peace, and they got it at a high price. Under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed on 3 March 1918, Soviet Russia gave up Poland, the Baltic lands, Finland and Ukraine, with a large share of the empire's population, industry and farmland. The Left SRs left the government in protest. The government moved the capital from Petrograd to Moscow.

A civil war followed from 1918 to about 1921. The White armies, led by former tsarist officers such as Anton Denikin and Admiral Alexander Kolchak, fought the Red Army that Trotsky built from scratch. Britain, France, the United States, Japan and others sent troops, though in limited numbers. There were also Ukrainian, Polish, Finnish, Baltic and Caucasian independence movements, peasant 'Green' armies and the anarchist forces of Nestor Makhno. In July 1918 the local Bolsheviks in Yekaterinburg shot Nicholas II, Alexandra, their five children and four servants. Both sides used terror, and after an attempt on Lenin's life in August 1918 the Cheka launched the 'Red Terror'. Grain requisitioning under 'war communism' set off peasant revolts and contributed to the famine of 1921–22. Estimates of the total number of deaths from fighting, terror, hunger and epidemics in these years run into several million.

The Reds won, largely because they held the industrial centre and the railways, were united, and could present themselves as defenders against foreign invaders and the return of landlords. But by 1921 the economy had collapsed. In March 1921 the sailors of Kronstadt, once heroes of 1917, rebelled and demanded soviets without Bolshevik domination. The revolt was crushed. At the same party congress Lenin introduced the New Economic Policy, which allowed peasants to sell their grain and small businesses to operate, and banned organised factions inside the party. The Soviet Union was formally created in December 1922. After Lenin's death in January 1924, Stalin outmanoeuvred Trotsky and his other rivals and by 1929 had begun forced collectivisation and a far more brutal dictatorship.

sections.title: Revolution from below or coup from above?

blocks.text: Historians have argued about 1917 since it happened. During the Cold War, many Western historians, such as Richard Pipes, described October as a coup by a small, conspiratorial party that hijacked a democratic revolution, and saw Stalin's terror as growing directly from Lenin's methods. Official Soviet history described it as the inevitable victory of the working class led by its party.

From the 1970s, social historians such as Sheila Fitzpatrick, Alexander Rabinowitch and S. A. Smith studied factories, regiments and villages, and argued that the Bolsheviks came to power because they expressed what millions of workers, soldiers and peasants actually wanted in the autumn of 1917, even if most of those people did not want a one-party dictatorship. Rabinowitch showed that the Bolshevik party in Petrograd was much less disciplined and more responsive to its members than the old picture suggested. Many historians now hold both views at once: October rested on real popular support for 'all power to the soviets', and the Bolsheviks then used that support to build a state that silenced the soviets themselves.

For someone thinking about social movements today, 1917 offers several lessons. It shows how fast an apparently powerful state can collapse when its army and its own officials stop believing in it, and how a group that offers simple answers to urgent needs can overtake broader coalitions that keep postponing decisions. It also shows how promises made to women, workers and peasants can be undone when a movement takes power without institutions that let those people hold it to account.

sections.title: Could the Provisional Government have survived?

blocks.text: Imagine you were advising the Provisional Government in April 1917. It faced a war it could not win, peasants who wanted land immediately, and an election it kept delaying. Which single decision, such as making a separate peace, holding the Constituent Assembly elections in the spring, or passing land reform at once, do you think would have given it the best chance of surviving, and what would that decision have cost?

fun_fact.title: The October Revolution happened in November
fun_fact.text: Because Russia used the Julian calendar until February 1918, the 'February' Revolution began on 8 March and the 'October' Revolution took place on 7 November by the Western calendar. After the Soviet government switched calendars, the anniversary of October was celebrated every year on 7 November, with parades on Red Square. The same calendar gap explains why the women's strike of 23 February 1917 fell on International Women's Day, 8 March.

glossary.explain: The two revolutions of 1917 in Russia: the February Revolution that ended the monarchy and the October Revolution that brought the Bolsheviks to power.
The uprising in Petrograd from 23 February to 2 March 1917 (Old Style) that ended with Nicholas II's abdication.
The Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd on 24–26 October 1917 (6–8 November, Western calendar).
The older calendar used in Russia until February 1918, thirteen days behind the Western Gregorian calendar in 1917.
The family that ruled Russia from 1613 to 1917.
A system in which one ruler holds unlimited power; the official principle of tsarist government.
The elected Russian parliament created after 1905, with limited powers.
Russian for 'council': an elected council of workers', soldiers' or peasants' delegates.
The council of workers' and soldiers' deputies formed in the capital on 27 February 1917.
The government that ruled Russia from March to October 1917, meant to last until a Constituent Assembly met.
Lenin's term for the sharing of authority between the Provisional Government and the soviets in 1917.
The Petrograd Soviet's order of 1 March 1917 telling soldiers to form committees and obey the Soviet.
Lenin's faction of the Russian Social Democrats, later the Communist Party.
The more moderate faction of the Russian Social Democrats, led by Julius Martov.
The peasant-oriented socialist party, the largest party in the 1917 Constituent Assembly elections.
The radical wing of the SRs that briefly joined the Bolshevik government.
The main liberal party in late imperial and revolutionary Russia.
Educated Russians who saw themselves as responsible for discussing and changing society.
The shooting of peaceful marchers in St Petersburg on 9 January 1905.
The year of strikes, mutinies and uprisings that forced Nicholas II to create the Duma.
Nicholas II's 1905 promise of civil liberties and an elected parliament.
Lenin's programme of April 1917 calling for no support for the Provisional Government and all power to the soviets.
The Petrograd railway station where Lenin arrived from exile on 3 April 1917.
The train in which the German government let Lenin and other exiles cross Germany in 1917.
The Bolsheviks' main slogan in 1917.
The Bolshevik slogan demanding that the soviets replace the Provisional Government.
Failed armed demonstrations in Petrograd in early July 1917.
General Kornilov's failed move on Petrograd in late August 1917.
Armed workers' militias that defended Petrograd and supported the October seizure of power.
The Petrograd Soviet body that organised the October seizure of power.
The tsars' palace in Petrograd, seat of the Provisional Government in October 1917.
The naval cruiser that fired a blank shot as a signal on the night of the October Revolution.
The former girls' school that served as Bolshevik and Soviet headquarters in 1917.
The national congress of soviets that approved the new Bolshevik government on 25–26 October 1917.
The Soviet government created in October 1917, chaired by Lenin.
The first Soviet decree, calling for an immediate end to the war.
The Soviet decree handing landlords' estates to peasant committees.
The elected assembly meant to write Russia's constitution; it met once in January 1918 and was dispersed.
The Soviet political police founded in December 1917.
The campaign of mass arrests and executions by the Cheka from 1918.
The March 1918 peace with Germany and its allies in which Soviet Russia gave up large territories.
The war of 1918–1921 between the Reds, Whites and many other forces.
The anti-Bolshevik armies of the civil war.
The Soviet army built by Trotsky in 1918.
The Soviet economic policy of 1918–1921, including grain requisitioning.
The March 1921 revolt of sailors at the naval base near Petrograd.
Lenin's 1921 policy allowing private trade and small business.
The Communist Party's women's department, 1919–1930.
The leading liberal women's suffrage organisation in Russia, which organised the 19 March 1917 march.
The socialist women's holiday, fixed on 8 March after the 1917 strike in Petrograd.
The women's military unit formed by Maria Bochkareva in 1917.

glossary.term: Ten Days That Shook the World
glossary.explain: John Reed's 1919 eyewitness book on the October Revolution.
Sergei Eisenstein's 1927 film about the October Revolution.
Warren Beatty's 1981 film about John Reed and Louise Bryant.
Kollontai's 1923 essay on love under socialism.
Kollontai's 1923 collection of stories about love and women's lives after the revolution.
A group inside the Communist Party in 1920–21 that wanted more power for trade unions.
The brief restoration of Puyi as emperor of China in July 1917.
The 1918 wave of protests in Japan over soaring rice prices.
The Allied military intervention in Siberia, 1918–1922, in which Japan sent the largest force.
The 1921 organisation of Taiwanese intellectuals pushing for cultural and political rights under Japanese rule.
Britain's November 1917 statement supporting a Jewish national home in Palestine.
The constitution adopted during the Mexican Revolution, with strong social and land rights.
The last tsar of Russia, who ruled from 1894.
The German-born empress, a granddaughter of Queen Victoria.
A Siberian peasant mystic who gained the trust of the imperial family because he seemed to help their haemophiliac son.
Leader of the Bolsheviks and the main architect of the October Revolution.
A brilliant speaker and writer who led the St Petersburg Soviet in 1905, joined the Bolsheviks in 1917 and organised the October seizure of power.
A lawyer and SR politician who was the only socialist in the first Provisional Government and became its prime minister in July 1917.
A liberal prince known for organising local government and wartime relief, and the first head of the Provisional Government from March to July 1917..
A historian and leader of the liberal Kadet party.
The leader of the Mensheviks and Lenin's former close friend.
The main thinker of the Socialist Revolutionary party and minister of agriculture in 1917.
The army commander-in-chief whose move on Petrograd in August 1917 failed.
A Bolshevik writer and organiser and the leading Marxist theorist of women's liberation in Russia.
A French-born Bolshevik, close collaborator of Lenin, and the first head of the Zhenotdel, the party's women's department.
Lenin's wife and political partner, a specialist in education who worked on literacy and schooling in the Soviet government..
A peasant woman who served in the tsar's army and in 1917 formed the Women's Battalion of Death to shame male soldiers into fighting.
A Polish-born revolutionary who founded and led the Cheka, the Soviet political police..
A Georgian Bolshevik who was People's Commissar for Nationalities after October.
The Orthodox priest who led the march of Bloody Sunday in January 1905.
An American journalist who witnessed the October Revolution and wrote Ten Days That Shook the World, published in 1919.
The Soviet film director whose October (1927) created the most famous images of the storming of the Winter Palace.
A senior Bolshevik who opposed the October uprising in advance.
A senior Bolshevik who joined Kamenev in opposing the uprising.
German socialist who proposed International Women's Day in 1910.
Tsarist prime minister, assassinated in 1911.
American journalist and John Reed's partner, who also reported from Russia.
Chinese intellectual who wrote early essays on the Bolshevik revolution and co-founded the CCP.
Ukrainian anarchist commander in the civil war.
White general in southern Russia.
Admiral who led the Whites in Siberia.
American historian who saw October as a coup.
Historian of Soviet social history.
Historian of the Bolsheviks in Petrograd in 1917.
